newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland appoints controversial public TV board.
newsitem.headline: Poland appoints controversial public TV board.

text.p: Poland's media authorities on Thursday appointed people linked to ruling coalition political parties to public television's new supervisory board, raising concern over news media freedom before next month's parliamentary elections.

The new nine-member board cleared by the National Radio and Television Council (KRRiT), the electronic media watchdog, included seven people connected with the parties in power, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance and the Peasant Party.
"People connected to the ruling coalition have a seven-person controlling package and can do what they want. This does not augur well," said KRRiT head Boleslaw Sulik.

Sulik, linked to the opposition, was outvoted by KRRiT members rooted in the ex-communist and Peasant parties, who on Thursday also pushed their people through to the supervisory board of public radio.
The board of public television, the main source of news in Poland, appoints the management, which shapes programme policies and controls finances.
A KRRIT member linked to the ex-communist party, Witold Grabos, said the new television board members were not politicians but experts.
"It is good that experts have been chosen and not politicians from the first echelons," the domestic news agency PAP quoted Grabos as saying.

Poland's parliamentary polls have been set for September 21 and many opposition politicians fear the ruling coalition, already wielding strong power in television, will use it in the election campaign.
The extent of independence of public television has been questioned by the European Union and the United States after Peasant-linked Ryszard Miazek was appointed its president.

Concern was also voiced earlier this year by a group of journalists and other employees who published a letter protesting alleged attempts to politicise public television and the chaos stemming from frequent management changes.
The changes in public television began last year when right-leaning head Wieslaw Walendziak quit, alleging he had been pressured by the two ruling parties.
Since then many senior television managers have quit or been sacked and some hard-hitting current affairs programmes associated with the former management have been scrapped.
KRRIT was created in the early 1990s to safeguard the electronic media's independence, which was seen as crucial after the fall of communism in 1989, and regulate the market.
But many analysts and politicians say the Council has fallen prone to political influence because its members are elected by parliament and the president.
